title: The rise of the public park
context: You will hear part of an urban history lecture about the development of public parks in nineteenth-century Britain.

lines.t: Today we're continuing our series on the industrial city by looking at something we tend to take completely for granted, and that's the public park. It's easy to assume that cities have always had open green spaces for everyone to use. But in fact the public park, as we know it, is largely an invention of the nineteenth century.

Before about eighteen forty, the green spaces in British towns were overwhelmingly private. There were royal parks, which the public could sometimes enter at the monarch's pleasure, and there were the elegant garden squares built for wealthy residents. Those squares were usually surrounded by railings, and only the people who lived around them were given a key. So for the great mass of factory workers crowded into the new industrial districts, there was simply nowhere green to go.

So why did that change? Historians usually point to three motives. The first was health. At the time, many doctors believed that diseases such as cholera were spread by bad air, rising from rubbish and sewage. If that was the case, then open spaces where fresh air could circulate seemed like an obvious remedy. Parks were very often described in this period as the lungs of the city, and that phrase appears again and again in parliamentary reports.

The second motive was what we might call moral. Middle-class reformers worried about how working people spent their limited free time, and in particular about drinking. A park was seen as a respectable alternative to the pubs, a place where families could take a walk together on a Sunday afternoon. The term used at the time was rational recreation.

The third motive is less often mentioned, but I'd argue it was just as important, and that's money. Take Birkenhead Park, near Liverpool, which opened in eighteen forty-seven and is often described as the first park in the world created with public money for public use. The council bought far more land than it needed for the park itself, and then sold off the plots around the edge for housing. Because people were willing to pay a premium to live next to the park, those sales covered most of the cost of building it.

Let's think for a moment about what these early parks looked like. The designers rejected straight lines and formal flower beds in favour of winding paths and irregular lakes, which were meant to imitate the countryside. A clever detail is that the soil dug out to create the lakes wasn't wasted. It was piled up to form small artificial hills, which gave visitors the sense of a varied landscape and also blocked views of the surrounding streets.

But this was not a space of total freedom. Victorian parks came with long lists of rules, and they were enforced by uniformed park keepers. Visitors could be thrown out for being badly dressed, for swearing, and very commonly for gambling, which was a particular concern of the authorities. Interestingly, the use of the grass was often restricted too. In many parks you could look at the lawns but not walk on them.

Towards the end of the century, the character of parks began to shift. There was a growing demand for sport, especially football, cricket and later tennis, and councils responded by setting aside large areas as playing fields. Around the same time, the first playgrounds with swings and climbing frames appeared, reflecting new ideas about the importance of play in children's development.

The twentieth century, however, was much less kind to parks. During the Second World War, the iron railings around many parks were cut down and taken away, officially to be melted down for weapons, though it's now thought that much of the metal was never actually used. After the war, budgets for maintenance were steadily reduced. Resident park keepers were replaced by mobile teams who visited occasionally, and many parks became neglected and associated with vandalism.

Since the nineteen nineties, there's been something of a revival. National lottery funding has paid for the restoration of hundreds of historic parks, including Birkenhead. But the day-to-day survival of many parks now depends on local volunteers, often organised into groups calling themselves the Friends of the park, who do everything from planting to fundraising. Whether that's a sustainable model is something I'd like you to think about before next week's seminar.
